---
title = "Performing administration tasks on the server side with a secret key"
github_url = "https://github.com/orgs/supabase/discussions/15860"
date_created = "2023-07-18T12:25:03+00:00"
topics = [ "auth", "platform" ]
keywords = [ "secret-key", "server", "security" ]
database_id = "0d3389c0-5e75-473c-a18b-0699d0911fb2"
---

By default, server side rendering (SSR) does not permit the use of a `secret` key. This restriction is in place to prevent the accidental exposure of your `secret` key to the public. Since SSR runs on both the server and client side, it becomes challenging to separate the key specifically for client-side usage.

However, there is a solution. You can create a separate Supabase client using the `createClient` method from `@supabase/supabase-js` and provide it with the `secret` key. In a server environment, you also need to disable certain properties to ensure proper functionality. See the example code below for the required settings.

By implementing this approach, you can safely use the `secret` key without compromising security or exposing sensitive information to the public.

```ts
import { createClient } from '@supabase/supabase-js'

const supabase = createClient(supabaseUrl, secretKey, {
  auth: {
    persistSession: false,
    autoRefreshToken: false,
    detectSessionInUrl: false,
  },
})
```

The `@supabase/ssr` package helps you do this for JavaScript/TypeScript applications. 7 8 ## Install 9 10 Install the `@supabase/supabase-js` and `@supabase/ssr` helper packages: 11 12 13 14 15 16 ```bash 17 npm install @supabase/supabase-js @supabase/ssr 18 ``` 19 20 21 22 23 24 ```bash 25 yarn add @supabase/supabase-js @supabase/ssr 26 ``` 27 28 29 30 31 32 ```bash 33 pnpm add @supabase/supabase-js @supabase/ssr 34 ``` 35 36 37 38 39 40 ## Set environment variables 41 42 Create a `.env.local` file in the project root directory. VITE_SUPABASE_URL=supabase_project_url 167 VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY=supabase_publishable_key 168 ``` 169 170 171 172 173 ## Create a client 174 175 {/* TODO: Can this be consolidated? */} 176 You need setup code to configure a Supabase client to use cookies. Once you have the utility code, you can use the `createClient` utility functions to get a properly configured Supabase client. 177 178 Use the browser client in code that runs on the browser, and the server client in code that runs on the server. 179 180 <$Partial path="auth_methods.mdx" /> 181 182 189 190 191 ### Write utility functions to create Supabase clients 192 193 To access Supabase from a Next.js app, you need 2 types of Supabase clients: 194 195 1. **Client Component client** - To access Supabase from Client Components, which run in the browser. 196 2. **Server Component client** - To access Supabase from Server Components, Server Actions, and Route Handlers, which run only on the server. 197 198 Since Next.js Server Components can't write cookies, you need a [Proxy](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/getting-started/proxy) to refresh expired Auth tokens and store them. 199 200 The Proxy is responsible for: 201 202 1. Refreshing the Auth token by calling `supabase.auth.getClaims()`. 203 2. Passing the refreshed Auth token to Server Components, so they don't attempt to refresh the same token themselves. This is accomplished with `request.cookies.set`. 204 3. Passing the refreshed Auth token to the browser, so it replaces the old token. This is accomplished with `response.cookies.set`. 205 206 <$Partial path="auth_methods.mdx" /> 207 208 209 210 214 215 The cookies object lets the Supabase client know how to access the cookies, so it can read and write the user session data. To make `@supabase/ssr` framework-agnostic, the cookies methods aren't hard-coded. These utility functions adapt `@supabase/ssr`'s cookie handling for Next.js. 216 217 `setAll` is called whenever the library needs to write cookies, for example after a token refresh. It receives two arguments: the array of cookies to set, and a `headers` object containing cache headers (`Cache-Control`, `Expires`, `Pragma`) that must be applied to the HTTP response to prevent CDNs from caching the response and leaking the session to other users. In the Proxy, apply these headers to the response. In Server Components, the headers cannot be set, which is why the `setAll` call is wrapped in a try/catch and the error is ignored. The Proxy handles writing cookies and headers on every request. 218 219 The cookie is named `sb--auth-token` by default. 220 221 222 223 227 228 Yes! Creating a Supabase client is lightweight. 229 230 - On the server, it basically configures a `fetch` call. You need to reconfigure the fetch call anew for every request to your server, because you need the cookies from the request. 231 - On the client, `createBrowserClient` already uses a singleton pattern, so you only ever create one instance, no matter how many times you call your `createClient` function. 232 233 234 235 236 237 Create a `lib/supabase` folder at the root of your project, or inside the `./src` folder if you are using one, with a file for each type of client. Then copy the lib utility functions for each client type. 238 239
240 <$CodeTabs> 241 <$CodeSample 242 path="/auth/nextjs/lib/supabase/client.ts" 243 meta="name=lib/supabase/client.ts" 244 language="typescript" 245 /> 246 <$CodeSample 247 path="/auth/nextjs/lib/supabase/server.ts" 248 meta="name=lib/supabase/server.ts" 249 language="typescript" 250 /> 251 252
253 254 ### Hook up proxy 255 256 The code adds a [matcher](https://nextjs.org/docs/app/api-reference/file-conventions/proxy#matcher) so the Proxy doesn't run on routes that don't access Supabase. 257 258 259 260 Be careful when protecting pages. The server gets the user session from the cookies, which can be spoofed by anyone. 261 262 Always use `supabase.auth.getClaims()` to protect pages and user data. 263 264 _Never_ trust `supabase.auth.getSession()` inside server code such as Proxy. It isn't guaranteed to revalidate the Auth token. 265 266 It's safe to trust `getClaims()` because it validates the JWT signature against the project's published public keys every time. 267 268 269 270 <$Partial path="auth_methods.mdx" /> 271 272
273 <$CodeTabs> 274 <$CodeSample path="/auth/nextjs/proxy.ts" meta="name=proxy.ts" language="typescript" /> 275 <$CodeSample 276 path="/auth/nextjs/lib/supabase/proxy.ts" 277 meta="name=lib/supabase/proxy.ts" 278 language="typescript" 279 /> 280 281
282 283 ## Congratulations 284 285 You're done! To recap, you've successfully: 286 287 - Called Supabase from a Server Action. 288 - Called Supabase from a Server Component. 289 - Set up a Supabase client utility to call Supabase from a Client Component. You can use this if you need to call Supabase from a Client Component, for example to set up a realtime subscription. 290 - Set up Proxy to automatically refresh the Supabase Auth session. 291 292 You can now use any Supabase features from your client or server code! 293 294 295 296 297 ### Set up server-side hooks 298 299 Set up server-side hooks in `src/hooks.server.ts`. The hooks: 300 301 - Create a request-specific Supabase client, using the user credentials from the request cookie. This client is used for server-only code. 302 - Check user authentication. 303 - Guard protected pages. 304 305 <$Partial path="auth_methods.mdx" /> 306 307 <$CodeSample 308 path="/auth/sveltekit/src/hooks.server.ts" 309 meta="name=src/hooks.server.ts" 310 language="typescript" 311 /> 312 313 To prevent TypeScript errors, add type definitions for the new event.locals properties. 314 315 <$CodeSample 316 path="/auth/sveltekit/src/app.d.ts" 317 meta="name=src/app.d.ts" 318 language="typescript" 319 /> 320 321 ### Create a Supabase client in your root layout 322 323 Create a Supabase client in your root `+layout.ts`. This client can be used to access Supabase from the client or the server. In order to get access to the Auth token on the server, use a `+layout.server.ts` file to pass in the session from event.locals. 324 325 Page components can access the Supabase client from the `data` object using the `load` function. 326 327 <$CodeTabs> 328 <$CodeSample 329 path="/auth/sveltekit/src/routes/+layout.ts" 330 meta="name=src/routes/+layout.ts" 331 language="typescript" 332 /> 333 334 <$CodeSample 335 path="/auth/sveltekit/src/routes/+layout.server.ts" 336 meta="name=src/routes/+layout.server.ts" 337 language="typescript" 338 /> 339 340 341 ## Congratulations 342 343 You're done! To recap, you've successfully: 344 345 - Set up server-side hooks to create a request-specific Supabase client and guard protected pages. 346 - Created a Supabase client in your root layout to use on both the client and server. 347 348 You can now use any Supabase features from your client or server code! 349 350 351 352 353 By default, Astro apps are static. This means the requests for data happen at build time, rather than when the user requests a page. At build time, there is no user, session or cookies. Therefore, we need to configure Astro for Server-side Rendering (SSR) if you want data to be fetched dynamically per request. 354 355 ```js astro.config.mjs 356 import { defineConfig } from 'astro/config' 357 358 export default defineConfig({ 359 output: 'server', 360 }) 361 ``` 362 363 370 371 372 ```ts index.astro 373 --- 374 import { createServerClient, parseCookieHeader } from "@supabase/ssr"; 375 376 const supabase = createServerClient( 377 import.meta.env.PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, 378 import.meta.env.PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, 379 { 380 cookies: { 381 getAll() { 382 return parseCookieHeader(Astro.request.headers.get('Cookie') ?? '') 383 }, 384 setAll(cookiesToSet, headers) { 385 cookiesToSet.forEach(({ name, value }) => 386 Astro.cookies.set(name, value)) 387 Object.entries(headers).forEach(([key, value]) => 388 Astro.response.headers.set(key, value) 389 ) 390 }, 391 }, 392 } 393 ); 394 --- 395 ``` 396 397 398 399 400 401 ```html index.astro 402 410 ``` 411 412 413 414 415 416 ```ts route.ts 417 import { createServerClient, parseCookieHeader } from "@supabase/ssr"; 418 import type { APIContext } from "astro"; 419 420 export async function GET(context: APIContext) { 421 const supabase = createServerClient( 422 import.meta.env.PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, 423 import.meta.env.PUBLIC_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, 424 { 425 cookies: { 426 getAll() { 427 return parseCookieHeader(context.request.headers.get('Cookie') ?? Unlike Next.js, this means you don't need a proxy or middleware layer to keep sessions fresh — the server client reads and writes the session cookie directly on each request. 840 841 Create a `lib/supabase` folder at the root of your project, or inside the `./src` folder if you are using one, then add a file for each type of client: 842 843 1. **Create a browser client in `lib/supabase/client.ts`.** Use it to access Supabase from components that run in the browser. 844 2. **Create a server client in `lib/supabase/server.ts`.** Use it to access Supabase from loaders, server functions, and other code that runs only on the server. 845 846 <$Partial path="auth_methods.mdx" /> 847 848 Copy the lib utility functions below into each file: 849 850
851 <$CodeTabs> 852 <$CodeSample 853 path="/auth/tanstack/lib/supabase/client.ts" 854 meta="name=lib/supabase/client.ts" 855 language="typescript" 856 /> 857 <$CodeSample 858 path="/auth/tanstack/lib/supabase/server.ts" 859 meta="name=lib/supabase/server.ts" 860 language="typescript" 861 /> 862 863
864 865 ### Protecting routes 866 867 TanStack Start has no global middleware layer, so protect each route explicitly. 868 869 To protect your routes: 870 871 1. Write a server function, `fetchClaims`, that calls `supabase.auth.getClaims()` and returns the claims, or `null` if the session isn't valid. 872 1. Call `fetchClaims` from a layout route's `beforeLoad` hook — for example, `_protected.tsx` — before any nested route renders, and redirect to `/login` when it returns `null`. 873 874 875 876 Skipping the check inside the server function exposes private data to unauthenticated users. `beforeLoad` runs on the server for the initial request and on the client for later navigation, but either way it only gates the route's render — it doesn't stop the server function from being called directly. Because there's no proxy re-checking every request, the server function is the only checkpoint that always runs, so it must call `supabase.auth.getClaims()` to authorize the request itself. 877 878 879 880 `getClaims()` validates the JWT signature on every call, the same check the Next.js Proxy relies on. Calling it inside the server function gives TanStack Start's per-route check that same guarantee, because the function runs on every request to a protected route. 881 882
883 <$CodeTabs> 884 <$CodeSample 885 path="/auth/tanstack/lib/supabase/fetch-claims-server-fn.ts" 886 meta="name=lib/supabase/fetch-claims-server-fn.ts" 887 language="typescript" 888 /> 889 <$CodeSample 890 path="/auth/tanstack/routes/_protected.tsx" 891 meta="name=routes/_protected.tsx" 892 language="typescript" 893 /> 894 895
896 897 Any other server function that returns or mutates private data needs this same check. Don't rely on a route being nested under `_protected` alone. 898 899 ## Congratulations 900 901 You're done! To recap, you've successfully: 902 903 - Set up a Supabase client utility to call Supabase from a browser component. You can use this if you need to call Supabase from the browser, for example to set up a realtime subscription. 904 - Set up a server client utility to call Supabase from loaders and server functions. 905 - Protected a route with `beforeLoad`, backed by a server function that authorizes the request itself. 906 907 You can now use any Supabase features from your client or server code! 908 909 910 911 912 ## Caching considerations 913 914 If your app uses ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration) or is deployed behind a CDN, caching of HTTP responses can cause users to receive another user's session. When a session is refreshed, the new token is written to the response via `Set-Cookie`. If that response is cached and served to a different user, that user will be signed in as the wrong person. 915 916 See the [advanced Auth server-side rendering guide](/docs/guides/auth/server-side/advanced-guide#can-i-use-server-side-rendering-with-a-cdn-or-cache) for details and framework-specific examples. 917 918 ## Next steps 919 920 - Implement [Authentication using Email and Password](/docs/guides/auth/passwords) 921 - Implement [Authentication using OAuth](/docs/guides/auth/social-login) 922 - [Learn more about SSR](/docs/guides/auth/server-side/advanced-guide) 923

Not a bad pattern — it's the recommended one. Per `apps/docs/content/troubleshooting/performing-administration-tasks-on-the-server-side-with-the-servicerole-secret-BYM4Fa.mdx`, you create a **separate** client with the secret/service_role key (with `persistSession: false, autoRefreshToken: false, detectSessionInUrl: false`) specifically for admin tasks, kept apart from your normal user-scoped client.

Two clarifications on your snippet:
- Your first client (`supabaseUserClient`) shouldn't use the service_role key — it should use the publishable/anon key and be built per-request from the user's cookies/JWT (see `apps/docs/content/guides/auth/server-side/creating-a-client.mdx`, "Do I need to create a new client for every route?" — yes, it's lightweight, and each request needs its own client using that request's token).
- The admin client (service_role) bypasses RLS and never refreshes/persists a session, so an expired user token doesn't affect it at all — expiry only matters for the user-scoped client, which you should refresh/reject per normal auth flow, not by reusing the service role client.
